pages.summary: The frequency response as gain and phase over frequency: the Bode diagram.
body: `bode` gives the gain (absolute, not in dB) and the phase in degrees at frequencies in rad/s, as 1-by-1-by-n arrays for one input and output; drawn when nothing is asked for, gain in dB above and phase below over a logarithmic frequency axis. Unless given, the frequencies reach two decades beyond the poles and zeros; `{wmin, wmax}` gives a range. Several models are drawn together, each with an optional line style. `bodeplot` draws; `bodemag` draws the gain alone.

examples.title: Two lags and one

pages.summary: The frequency response in the complex plane, as gain against phase, and as singular values.
body: `nyquist` draws the response in the complex plane for positive frequencies and its mirror image for negative ones (dashed), with the critical point -1: the closed loop is stable when the curve encircles -1 counterclockwise once for each unstable open-loop pole. `nichols` draws the gain in dB against the phase in degrees. `sigma` gives the singular values of the response at each frequency, the gains of a model with several inputs and outputs in its most and least sensitive directions.
syntax: The singular values, a column for each frequency.

examples.title: A loop with a gain margin of 2.5
The gains of two inputs and two outputs

pages.summary: How far a loop is from instability: its gain and phase margins.
body: The gain margin is how much the loop gain can grow before the closed loop is unstable: 1/|L| where the phase crosses -180 degrees (at Wcg). The phase margin is how much more phase lag it can take: 180 degrees plus the phase where the gain crosses 1 (at Wcp). `margin` gives the smallest of them, or draws the Bode diagram with them marked and named in the title; `allmargin` gives every crossing, the delay margin (the phase margin over its frequency, the delay the loop can take) and whether the closed loop is stable.
syntax: The margins, the gain margin absolute.

pages.summary: The root locus: where the closed loop's poles go as the loop gain grows.
body: For a loop L in negative feedback with gain k, the closed-loop poles are the roots of den + k*num. They start at the open-loop poles (x) when k is 0 and end at the zeros (o), or go off to infinity along asymptotes, as k grows. `rlocus` draws the branches over gains spaced logarithmically, or gives the poles at the gains asked for (a column for each gain).

examples.title: A loop with three poles and a zero

pages.summary: A model given by its frequency response alone, as measured.
body: An `frd` model holds a response at a list of frequencies: ny-by-nu-by-n, or a vector for one input and output, the frequencies in rad/s unless `'FrequencyUnit'` is `'Hz'`. It adds, multiplies and divides with other models (each evaluated at its frequencies), closes loops with `feedback`, and is drawn by `bode` and `bodemag` at its own frequencies, the only ones it has. `frdata` gives the response and the frequencies back.

examples.title: A measured plant in a loop

pages.summary: Whether every state can be steered by the inputs, and seen in the outputs.
body: `ctrb` gives the controllability matrix [B, AB, A^2 B, ...] and `obsv` the observability matrix [C; CA; CA^2; ...]: the model is controllable (observable) when its rank is the number of states. `ctrbf` and `obsvf` transform the model orthogonally so that the states that cannot be steered (seen) come first: `k` gives how many controllable (observable) states each step of the staircase found, `sum(k)` of them in all.
syntax: [Abar, Bbar, Cbar, T, k] = ctrbf(A, B, C)
[Abar, Bbar, Cbar, T, k] = obsvf(A, B, C)

pages.summary: Lyapunov equations, and the Gramians and covariances they give.
body: `lyap` solves A X + X A' + Q = 0 (or the Sylvester equation A X + X B + C = 0), `dlyap` the discrete A X A' - X + Q = 0. For a stable model, `gram` gives the controllability Gramian (A Wc + Wc A' + B B' = 0), how strongly the inputs reach each state, or the observability Gramian. `covar` gives the steady output covariance of a model driven by white noise of intensity W, C Wc C' + D W D' with Wc the Gramian of B W B'.

examples.title: A stable pair of states

pages.summary: Algebraic Riccati equations, continuous and discrete.
body: `care` gives the stabilizing solution X of A'X + XA - (XB + S) R^-1 (B'X + S') + Q = 0, `dare` that of A'XA - X - (A'XB + S)(B'XB + R)^-1 (B'XA + S') + Q = 0, with R the identity and S zero unless given. L gives the closed-loop eigenvalues and G the gain: the solutions behind the linear-quadratic regulator and the Kalman filter.
syntax: [X, L, G] = care(A, B, Q, R, S)
With the eigenvalues and the gain.
[X, L, G] = dare(A, B, Q, R, S)

pages.summary: The linear-quadratic regulator: the state feedback that balances the states' size against the input's.
body: `lqr` gives the gain K of u = -Kx that makes the integral of x'Qx + u'Ru (+ 2x'Nu) smallest, with S the Riccati solution and P the closed-loop poles; of a discrete model, or with `dlqr`, the sum over samples. `lqry` weights the outputs, y'Qy, instead of the states. `lqi` adds integrators of the error r - y to the plant, so that the loop follows a constant reference with no error left: u = -K*[x; xi].
syntax: [K, S, P] = lqr(A, B, Q, R, N)
[K, S, e] = dlqr(A, B, Q, R)

examples.title: A double integrator, in time and sampled
Outputs weighted, and an integrator added
examples.code:
sys = ss([0 1; -2 -3], [0; 1], [1 0], 0);
Ky = lqry(sys, 10, 1)
lqr(sys, sys.C'*10*sys.C, 1)
Ki = lqi(sys, diag([1 1 10]), 1)

pages.summary: State estimators: the Kalman filter, and a regulator built from an estimator and a state feedback.
body: For x' = Ax + Bu + Gw, y = Cx + Du + v, with process noise w and measurement noise v of covariances Q and R, `lqe` gives the gain L of the estimator xhat' = A xhat + Bu + L(y - C xhat - Du) that makes the error's covariance P smallest. `kalman` builds that estimator from a model whose last inputs are the noise w: it takes [u; y] and gives [yhat; xhat]. `estim` builds an estimator from any gain; `reg` joins one to a state feedback K into a controller from y to u = -K xhat. By the separation principle the closed loop's poles are those of A - BK and of A - LC.
syntax: [L, P, E] = lqe(A, G, C, Q, R)

examples.title: An oscillator measured with noise

pages.summary: Pole placement: the state feedback that puts the closed loop's poles where they are asked for.
body: Both give K such that the poles of A - BK are p. `place` uses a robust method that also takes several inputs and keeps the gain well conditioned (no pole may be asked for more times than there are inputs); `acker` uses Ackermann's formula, for a single input, simple but ill-conditioned for many states.

pages.summary: The largest gain of a model over all frequencies: its H-infinity norm.
body: `getPeakGain` gives the largest singular value of the frequency response and the frequency where it is, found on a fine grid about the poles and zeros and each peak refined. `hinfnorm` gives the same for a stable model, and Inf for an unstable one, whose response to a bounded input grows without bound.
syntax: The peak gain and its frequency.

examples.title: A resonance against its formula

pages.summary: Model reduction: the states that matter least to the input-output behaviour, left out.
body: The Hankel singular values (`hsvd`) measure how much each state of a balanced realization takes part in the response: `balreal` gives that realization, in which the controllability and observability Gramians are both diag(g). `balred` keeps the r states of the largest values and leaves out the rest, by default with their derivatives set to zero so that the gain at rest is kept (`'Truncate'` drops them). `modred` leaves out the states named, of any realization.
syntax: r states, the gain at rest kept.
